subject: Biotechnology
title: DNA Data Storage
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on DNA Data Storage.

hook.text: All the world's data could fit in a room full of DNA — nature's storage medium outlasts any hard drive.

buildup.text: Binary data is converted to base sequences — four letters give DNA twice the information density of binary.

discovery.text: Researchers stored an entire movie, an operating system, and a $50 gift card in DNA — then read it back perfectly.

twist.text: Write speed is the bottleneck — DNA synthesis is a million times slower than writing to a hard drive.

climax.text: DNA lasts thousands of years in cool, dry conditions — woolly mammoth genomes survived 10,000 years in permafrost.

punchline.text: Write data in DNA — the oldest storage medium becomes the newest.

quiz.question: What is the biggest limitation of DNA data storage currently?
options: DNA degrades too quickly to store data long-term
Writing data to DNA is extremely slow compared to electronic storage
Only text can be stored in DNA, not images or video

details.summary: DNA can store digital information at extraordinary density because each nucleotide base encodes two bits of data. Researchers have stored entire books, videos, and operating systems in DNA molecules that can theoretically preserve data for thousands of years in a tiny volume.
details.whyItMatters: Global data generation is outpacing storage capacity. DNA stores a million times more data per volume than hard drives and lasts thousands of years without power.
takeaways: DNA encodes digital data by mapping binary to nucleotide base sequences
One gram of DNA can theoretically store 215 petabytes of data
DNA data remains readable for thousands of years under proper storage conditions

faq.question: How is digital data encoded into DNA?
faq.answer: Binary data is converted to nucleotide sequences using encoding schemes that map bits to bases. The sequences are synthesized as short DNA oligonucleotides with index sequences for ordering. Reading back involves sequencing the DNA and decoding the base sequence to binary.

faq.question: When will DNA data storage become commercially practical?
faq.answer: The main barriers are cost and speed of DNA synthesis and sequencing. Current synthesis costs make DNA storage only viable for archival data that is written once and read rarely. Costs would need to drop roughly a thousandfold for broad commercial viability.
